answer: As stated in [S2], commercial banks must additionally consider 'other UNSCRs' and 'lists in the first schedule and the fourth schedule of UAPA, 1967' for sanctions compliance. These refer to other United Nations Security Council resolutions and specific domestic schedules under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, required for implementation of section 51A of the UAPA and section 12A of the WMD Act. [S2] explicitly lists these as additional requirements beyond those previously outlined.

According to [S1], commercial banks must ensure adherence to the provisions of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010, and the Rules made thereunder. Furthermore, they must ensure meticulous compliance with any instructions or communications issued from time to time by the RBI, based on advice received from the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India.

According to [S1], commercial banks must review their money laundering and terrorist financing risk assessment at least annually. [S1] explicitly states: "However, the bank shall review it at least annually."

[S1] states that the bank shall temporarily cease operations in the account until the customer submits the PAN or equivalent e-document thereof or Form No. 60. Before temporarily ceasing operations, the bank shall give the customer an accessible notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard, and include appropriate relaxations in its internal policy for customers unable to provide the documents due to injury, illness, or old age, subject to enhanced monitoring.

According to [S4], a commercial bank must monitor the 'at par' cheque facility offered to co-operative banks and review the arrangements to assess credit risk and reputational risk. Furthermore, [S4] states that the bank retains the right to verify records maintained by co-operative banks/societies for compliance with KYC and AML instructions.

As per [S1], any remittance of funds by way of demand draft, mail/telegraphic transfer, NEFT, IMPS, or any other mode, and issue of travellers’ cheques for value of ₹50,000 and above shall be effected by debit to the customer’s account or against cheques and not against cash payment.

According to [S1] paragraph 61(1), a commercial bank should consider the FATF Statements circulated by the RBI from time to time and publicly available information for identifying countries that do not or insufficiently apply the FATF Recommendations.

Under the general restriction, a commercial bank must collect account payee cheques only for the payee constituent. [S1] states: "The bank shall not collect account payee cheques for any person other than the payee constituent." This means the payee constituent is the sole party for whom collection is permitted under the regulation.

[S1] states that the bank shall undertake countermeasures when called upon so to do by any international or intergovernmental organisation of which India is a member and which is accepted by the Central Government.

For a commercial bank, RBI's KYC requirements operate in addition to, rather than replace, obligations under other laws and regulations. Passage [S1] explicitly states that banks must carry out customer due diligence processes "in addition to" ensuring compliance with the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002 and the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA). This "in addition to and not in substitution of" principle is consistent across multiple RBI directions, indicating that KYC requirements supplement rather than supersede other regulatory obligations.

Yes, according to [S1] paragraph 26, a commercial bank may undertake V-CIP for CDD in case of new customer onboarding for individual customers, as well as for Beneficial Owners (BOs) in case of Legal Entity (LE) customers.
Under the RBI KYC Directions for Commercial Banks, para 31, the bank must obtain any two of the listed documents as proof of business/activity for a sole proprietary firm. [S1], para 31.

When a commercial bank opens a savings bank account for an SHG, it is not required to perform customer due diligence on every member, as [S1] states that the CDD of all the office bearers shall suffice. Therefore, only the due diligence of the office bearers is sufficient for account opening.
According to [S1], a commercial bank must categorise customers into low, medium, and high-risk categories based on its assessment and risk perception.

As per [S3] para 41(1), commercial banks must re-check the risk ratings assigned to customer accounts at least once every six months. The RBI KYC Directions mandate a periodic review of risk categorisation of accounts with such periodicity being at least once in every six months.
A commercial bank must disclose full-fledged information on its products and their implications to customers so they can make an informed judgment about their choice of products. [S1]

A commercial bank must establish a transparent policy for renewing overdue term deposits, which must be non-discretionary and non-discriminatory. The terms and conditions of renewal, including interest rates, must be notified to the customer at the time of acceptance of the deposit. [S1]

The RBI (Commercial Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 do not override or replace other existing laws or regulations applicable to commercial banks. As stated in para 466 [S5], the provisions of these Directions "shall be in addition to, and not in derogation of the provisions of any other laws, rules, regulations, or directions, for the time being in force."

[S1] states that the bank shall make available all printed material used by retail customers, including account opening forms, pay-in-slips, and passbooks, in trilingual form: English, Hindi, and the concerned Regional Language.

Per [S1], a commercial bank must ensure that necessary infrastructure and facilities are put in place and appropriate security measures are taken at each branch where loans are sanctioned against gold or silver collateral. The bank must also ensure that such collateral is handled only within its branches and only by its employees.

The interest rates on deposit accounts and related matters for commercial banks are governed by the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025, as established in [S2], confirmed in [S1] that banks must be guided by them, and clarified in [S4] that these 2025 Directions supersede all prior related instructions.
According to [S1], the bank should periodically organise Exporters' Meet at centres with concentration of exporters to facilitate interaction between the bank and exporters.

According to [S1], a commercial bank's policy must cover auction-related conduct aspects including the auction procedure specifying the trigger event and notice timeline [S1](3), the notice period allowed to borrower(s)/legal heir(s) for loan settlement before auction [S1](5), the empanelment of auctioneers [S1](6), and procedures for loss, deterioration, or discrepancy of collateral with fair compensation and timelines [S1](7). Additionally, [S5] requires that a bank declare a reserve price for the gold and silver collateral at auction, which shall not be less than 90 per cent of its current value, or 85 per cent if auctions fail twice.

According to [S1], a bank may provide additional facilities beyond the minimum BSBD account services, with or without charges, in a non-discretionary and non-discriminatory manner with transparent disclosure to the customer, provided the customer is not required to maintain a minimum balance. The availment of such additional facilities shall be strictly at the option of the customer.
According to [S1] para 192, the bank must undertake at least an annual review of accounts where there has been no customer-induced transaction for more than a year.

According to [S2], banks should give publicity in branches cautioning against dubious deposit schemes. [S1] adds that such messages may be displayed in bank branches (in the state's official language) and at ATMs or Business Correspondent Points for wider customer visibility.

Yes, a commercial bank is held responsible for the conduct of recovery agents it engages. [S1] explicitly states that "The bank, as principal, is responsible for the actions of its agents." [S4] further reinforces this by requiring the bank to ensure agents adhere to instructions and maintain due diligence processes during recovery.
As stated in [S1], a bank shall have "Enquiry" or "May I Help You" counters located near the entry point of the banking hall at all branches, excluding very small branches.
According to [S1], the prescribed post-shipment interest rate ceases from the date of credit to the 'Nostro' account.

As stated in [S1], the bank shall undertake special drives periodically to find out the whereabouts of the customers, their nominees or legal heirs in respect of inoperative accounts / unclaimed deposits.

A commercial bank must conduct regular audits of its outsourced service providers, including subcontractors, which may be performed by its internal or external auditors [S1]. These audits shall assess the service provider's performance, risk management practices, and compliance with laws and regulations, with frequency determined by the nature and extent of risk [S3]. The bank also retains the right to conduct audits and obtain relevant audit reports from the service provider [S4].

According to [S1], when a commercial bank appoints a group entity to perform outsourced services, the selection shall be based on objective reasons that are similar to the selection of a third-party, and the bank must appropriately deal with any conflicts of interest that such an arrangement may entail.

Per [S1], an NBFC bears responsibility for the conduct of DSAs/DMAs and recovery agents engaged through a service provider. Per [S2], a bank bears similar responsibility for such agents, as both retain ultimate control and are accountable for their actions and customer information confidentiality.

[S1] (para 54) states that a commercial bank must ensure a non-group service provider is not owned or controlled by any director, key managerial personnel, approver of the outsourcing arrangement, or their relatives. [S4] (para 18)(v) similarly prohibits such ownership or control for service providers that are not subsidiaries of the bank. An exception may be permitted only with the approval of the Board or a Committee of the Board, followed by appropriate disclosure, oversight, and monitoring, as provided in the proviso to [S1] and referenced in [S3] (para 13)(iv).

[S1] paragraph 65 states that sufficient compliance requires clear separation and isolation of the bank's data from its customers' specific data and information, ensuring only authorised bank personnel can access their respective data in a multi-tenant environment/architecture.

Yes, according to [S2], outsourcing arrangements "shall not affect the rights of its customers against the bank, including the ability of the customers to obtain redressal as applicable under relevant laws." [S3] further states that "responsibility for redressal of customers’ grievances related to outsourced services shall rest with the bank."
Under the RBI's 2025 outsourcing directions, commercial banks must include in their outsourcing agreements a clause granting the right to conduct audits

Yes, a commercial bank may outsource any IT service within its business group or conglomerate, provided that such an arrangement is backed by the Board-approved policy and appropriate SLAs / agreements with its group entities are in place. [S1]

[S1] explicitly allows commercial banks (as REs) to adopt a pooled (shared) audit when multiple REs use the same third-party IT service provider, instead of conducting separate audits. However, the REs remain responsible for ensuring that audit requirements related to their respective contracts with the service provider are met effectively. The passage states that REs can either pool their audit resources or engage an independent third-party auditor to jointly audit a common service provider.

According to paragraph 66 of the Commercial Banks directions, a bank must consider additional factors when evaluating a service provider for outsourced IT services, including technology and infrastructural stability, data backup and disaster recovery plans, conflict of interest, the provider’s capability to identify and segregate the bank’s data, information/cyber security risk assessment, appropriate controls and contractual arrangements for data protection and the bank’s access to data, the ability to service customers confidentially across multiple entities, and the ability to enforce agreements regarding data storage, protection, and confidentiality [S1].

Under [S1] paragraph 77, a commercial bank must create an inventory of IT services outsourced to service providers, including key entities involved in their supply chains. This inventory is a core requirement under the RBI's outsourcing risk management directions for commercial banks.

As stated in [S1], a commercial bank must consider the availability of alternative service providers or the possibility of bringing the outsourced activity back in-house in an emergency, along with the costs, time, and resources involved. [S1] specifies that these factors are essential for establishing a viable contingency plan.

According to [S1] para 11, the Board or a Committee of the Board to which powers have been delegated is responsible for putting in place a framework to evaluate the risks and materiality of all existing and prospective outsourcing arrangements.

Yes, the RBI outsourcing requirements apply to subcontracted activities. As stated in [S1], paragraph 4(2), the bank must obtain prior approval or consent before the service provider engages any subcontractor, and must review the subcontracting arrangement to ensure it complies with Chapter III Directions.

According to [S1], commercial banks shall not outsource core management functions including Internal Audit, the compliance function, and decision-making functions such as determining compliance with KYC norms for opening deposit accounts, giving sanction for loans (including retail loans), and management of investment portfolio.

A bank must establish a risk management framework that comprehensively addresses the identification, measurement, mitigation, management, and reporting of risks from IT outsourcing arrangements [S1]. Additionally, it must have a management structure to monitor and control outsourced services, including performance, uptime, service availability, SLA adherence, and incident response mechanisms [S2].

According to [S3], the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025 apply to Commercial Banks, defined as banking companies (other than Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, and Local Area Banks), corresponding new banks, and the State Bank of India, as defined under clauses (c), (da), and (nc) of Section 5 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

According to paragraph 84 of the Commercial Banks - Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct guidelines, card-issuers must ensure that their call centre staff are trained adequately to competently handle and escalate complaints, the Grievance Redressal process must include automatic escalation of unresolved complaints from the call center to higher authorities, and there must be a system for acknowledging customers' complaints for follow-up using complaint or docket numbers, even if received over the phone. [S1]

According to [S1] para 55, the co-branded card must explicitly indicate that it has been issued under a co-branding arrangement. Additionally, in all marketing and advertising material, the name of the card-issuer shall be clearly shown, and a commercial bank issuing such cards must ensure these requirements are met.

You must avoid intimidation or harassment of any kind, including humiliating publicly or intruding on the privacy of cardholders' family, referees, or friends, as well as making threatening anonymous calls or false/misleading representations [S3]. You and your collection agents must also refrain from actions that could damage your integrity and reputation and must observe strict customer confidentiality [S1]. Furthermore, all recovery efforts must adhere to the extant Fair Practices Code for lenders [S5].

As stated in [S1], prior approval of the Reserve Bank is not necessary for the issuance of co-branded debit cards, co-branded prepaid cards, and co-branded credit cards by commercial banks, subject to conditions stipulated under the chapter. [S1] further specifies that the co-branding arrangement must also comply with specific conditions applicable to such cards. Therefore, commercial banks do not need to obtain prior RBI approval for issuing co-branded cards, provided they adhere to the outlined conditions.

According to [S1](6), if no OTP-based consent is received for activating a credit card, the card-issuer must close the account within seven working days from the date of seeking confirmation from the customer.

According to paragraph 31 of the Master Direction for Commercial Banks [S1], the monetary threshold that triggers the requirement for explicit cardholder consent is the lower of one percent of the credit limit or ₹5,000, arising from refunds, failed, or reversed transactions for which payment has already been made by the cardholder.
The card-issuer shall explicitly bring to the notice of the customer that such information is being provided in terms of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005. [S1]

As stated in [S1], all communications issued by recovery agents must contain the name, email-id, telephone number and address of the concerned senior officer of the card-issuer whom the customer can contact.

According to [S2], a commercial bank may report a credit card account to credit information companies or impose late-payment charges only when the account remains overdue for more than three days, with the number of days computed from the payment due date mentioned in the credit card statement.

[S1] explicitly prohibits commercial banks from levying any charge not indicated to the cardholder at the time of issue and without their explicit consent, requiring all card-associated charges to be displayed on the issuer’s website. [S4] further states there shall be no hidden charges while issuing credit cards free of charge, and changes in charges require prospective effect with at least one month's prior notice. Thus, commercial banks may not levy undisclosed charges at issuance, except for subsequently imposed service taxes or government statutory charges.

Yes, according to [S1], commercial banks (card-issuers) may issue business credit cards to individuals for business expenses. The passage explicitly states: “Card-issuers may issue business credit cards to business entities / individuals for business expenses.”

A commercial bank's credit card issuance and conduct policy must be well-documented, approved by its Board or a delegated Committee, conform to RBI instructions and the Directions, and be available on the bank's website [S1]. Additionally, the policy must cover interest rate ceilings and other charges, procedures for reporting default status to a Credit Information Company, co-branding arrangements, standard operating procedures for discretionary blocking/deactivating/suspending cards, the time period for completing formalities after blocking a lost card, and a grievance redressal and compensation framework [S3].

As stated in [S1], card-issuers shall ensure that wrong bills are not raised and issued to cardholders. This requires commercial banks to validate all billing information before dispatching statements, thereby preventing inaccurate bills from reaching cardholders.

According to [S4], card-issuers shall make available to the cardholders in writing, a set of contractual terms and conditions governing the issue and use of such cards. These terms shall be expressed clearly and also maintain a fair balance between the interests of the parties concerned.

According to [S1], disclosure of customers’ information to DSAs, DMAs, and recovery agents is limited to the extent necessary for them to discharge their duties. Personal information provided by the cardholder but not required for recovery purposes shall not be released by the card-issuer.

Under [S1] para 42, a commercial bank has the freedom to determine the interest rate on deposits accepted or renewed under the RFC Account Scheme, provided it follows a comprehensive policy on interest rates on deposits duly approved by the Board of Directors or any Committee to which such powers have been delegated.

Per paragraph 11 of the RBI Directions, the bank must calculate interest on a prematurely withdrawn domestic term deposit at the rate applicable to the amount and period the deposit remained with the bank, not the contracted rate [S1]. Furthermore, no interest is payable if the withdrawal occurs before the minimum period specified in paragraph 10(1) [S1].
According to [S1], paragraph 27(i), the minimum tenor for NRE term deposits is one year and for NRO term deposits is seven days.

As stated in [S1], rupee deposits of non-residents under NRE and NRO accounts shall be accepted only by those banks that are authorised under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA) by the Reserve Bank of India from time to time.

Yes, as stated in [S1] para 12, a commercial bank may, at its discretion, pay additional interest of one per cent per annum over and above the scheduled rate on deposits held by its staff and their exclusive associations. This 1% is the maximum additional rate permitted for such deposits under the RBI guidelines.

According to [S1], a commercial bank must treat a deceased depositor's NRE term deposit as a domestic rupee term deposit at maturity if the claimant(s) are residents. In such cases, the deposit is treated as a domestic rupee term deposit and interest is paid for the subsequent period at the rate applicable to a domestic term deposit of similar maturity.

According to paragraph 41(1) of the Directions, if the components of penalty are not clearly brought to the notice of the depositor at the time of acceptance of the FCNR(B) deposit, then the exchange loss arising out of premature withdrawal shall be borne by the bank. [S1]

According to [S1], para 35(1), if an FCNR(B) deposit is renewed within 14 days of maturity, the interest rate payable is the lower of the rate prevailing on the date of maturity and the rate on the date the depositor seeks renewal.

Yes, according to [S1] para 46, any action taken under the previous Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions before their repeal shall continue to be governed by the provisions thereof.

A commercial bank is prohibited from charging a penalty for premature withdrawal of a domestic term deposit in the following cases: when the deposit is split at the request of claimants of deceased depositors or joint account holders without changing the period or aggregate amount [S1] para 24; upon the death of the depositor, allowing premature termination without penal charge even within a lock-in period [S4] para 296; and where depositors of branches mentioned in paragraph 7(9) seek premature withdrawal consequent to the transfer of

Yes, according to [S1] para 14, a bank may, at its discretion, give its resident Indian retired staff who are senior citizens the benefit of additional interest rates as admissible to senior citizens over and above the additional interest payable to them by virtue of their being retired members of the bank’s staff. This means such retired employees can receive the senior citizen interest benefit in addition to the staff retirement benefit, subject to the bank's discretion.

According to [S1], paragraph 21 states that interest on the minimum credit balance in the composite cash credit account of a farmer is paid "during the period from the 10th to the last day of each calendar month."

[S3] para 7(1) specifies that a Board-approved comprehensive policy must cover interest rates on deposits, penalties for premature withdrawal of term deposits (including partial), penalties for premature withdrawal of NRE term deposits, and penalties for premature withdrawal of FCNR(B) term deposits. [S4] para 22 further requires such a policy to address premature withdrawal of term deposits including partial premature withdrawal, while [S3] para 7(2) adds that interest rates must be uniform across all branches and customers without discrimination.
NOT FOUND

Banks may use foreign currency funds borrowed under Notification No. FEMA.3(R)/2018-RB and funds generated through buy-sell swaps in the domestic forex market for granting PCFC, subject to Aggregate Gap Limit adherence [S3]. Additionally, foreign currency balances in Exchange Earners Foreign Currency (EEFC) Accounts, Resident Foreign Currency Accounts (RFC(D)), and Foreign Currency (Non-Resident) Accounts (Banks) Scheme may be utilised for financing PCFC [S4].

According to [S1] para 264, the bank shall ensure that the final products are exported by the processors/exporters as per the terms and conditions of the sanction in order to liquidate the pre-shipment credit as per extant instructions.

According to [S1] para 439, the exposure of a bank by way of PCEs to bonds issued by each such NBFC / HFC shall be restricted to one per cent of capital funds of the RE within the extant single / group borrower exposure limits. This sets the maximum PCE exposure to a single NBFC or HFC at 1% of the bank's capital funds, subject to overall concentration norms. No other passage specifies a different per-entity limit for bank PCE to NBFC/HFC bonds.

According to [S1], all corporates and other constituent borrowers having a turnover above the threshold level fixed by the bank’s Board of Directors are mandated to disclose the aging schedule of their overdue payables in their periodical returns submitted to banks.

According to [S1] para 247, a commercial bank must grant export credit to exporters of good track record until the realization of proceeds from cheques or drafts received from abroad, provided the credit is against a genuine export order, aligns with trade practices for the goods in question, and is an approved method of realizing export proceeds under extant rules.

According to [S1], when a commercial bank introduces a new lending product, it must take into account the customer's suitability and appropriateness and ensure that borrowers/customers are made fully aware of the risks and liabilities under such products.

Before releasing funds, a commercial bank must ensure the borrower has obtained requisite statutory/regulatory clearances from government authorities [S2]. The bank must also verify the genuineness of title documents to the mortgaged property at the time of loan acceptance, not deferring this until recovery proceedings [S3]. Furthermore, funds shall not be released unless the builder/developer fulfils stipulated terms such as disclosing mortgagee banks and providing No Objection Certificates for property sales [S1].

According to [S1] para 119(1), when a commercial bank finances a specific housing or development project, the builder/developer/company must disclose in the pamphlets/brochures the name(s) of the bank(s) to which the property is mortgaged.
Yes, [S2] and [S1] both require that a commercial bank shall not enter into lease agreements departmentally with equipment leasing companies and other NBFCs engaged in equipment leasing.

As stated in [S1], bills rediscounted 'with recourse' in the domestic market are only reflected for the first bank discounting the bills, since that bank alone has recourse to the exporter, and the rediscounting bank shall not reckon the amount as export credit for reporting purposes.

According to [S1] para 41, gold or silver accepted as collateral shall be valued based on its actual purity (caratage), using the lower of the average closing price over the preceding 30 days or the previous day's closing price, as published by the India Bullion and Jewellers Association Ltd. (IBJA) or a SEBI-regulated commodity exchange. Furthermore, [S4] para 43 specifies that for valuation purposes, only the intrinsic value of the gold or silver contained in the eligible collateral shall be reckoned, excluding other cost elements such as precious stones or gems.

According to [S1], a microfinance loan is a collateral-free loan given to a household with annual income up to ₹3,00,000, where household is defined as an individual family unit (husband, wife, and unmarried children). [S2] expands this by stating that all collateral-free loans, irrespective of end use or mode of disbursal (physical or digital), provided to low-income households (income up to ₹3,00,000) are considered microfinance loans, and such loans must not be linked with a lien on the borrower's deposit account or backed by hypothecation of any security.

According to [S2], a commercial bank must capture and maintain project-specific data in electronic and easily accessible format on an ongoing basis. The bank is required to maintain a project finance database that, at a minimum, includes parameters such as debtor profile, original project profile, and changes in DCCO, as specified in the passage.

According to [S1], the bank shall not grant finance for the construction of buildings meant purely for Government / Semi-Government offices, including Municipal and Panchayat offices. Therefore, a commercial bank is not allowed to finance the construction of a building intended solely for a Municipal office, except for activities that will be refinanced by institutions like NABARD.

As a compliance officer at a commercial bank, you may accept DLG only in the forms specified in [S1]: (1) Cash deposited with the bank, (2) Fixed Deposit maintained with a Scheduled Commercial Bank with a lien marked in favour of the bank, and (3) Bank Guarantee in favour of the bank.

[S1] para 4.1 distinguishes the two: an Internet Banking Channel is a digital banking channel offered over the internet via web browser-based applications (excluding mobile applications), while a Mobile Banking Channel is offered using mobile applications, unstructured supplementary service data (USSD), and short message service (SMS) for operating accounts and accessing services.

Yes, under para 11 of the Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, 2025, the Reserve Bank may exempt any regulated entity from all or any provisions of the Directions, either generally or for a specified period, to avoid hardship or for other just and sufficient reasons, subject to conditions imposed by the Reserve Bank [S1].

According to [S1] para 9, banks must comply with the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, FEMA 1999, the Payment and Settlement Systems (PSS) Act, 2007, and KYC/AML/CFT directions issued by the Reserve Bank from time to time. The jurisdiction for legal settlement is within India.

Prior to launching a transactional banking facility, a commercial bank must obtain prior approval from the Reserve Bank of India and apply through the PRAVAAH portal to the Department of Regulation, RBI, along with the approval of the appropriate authority and necessary supporting documents. [S1]

As stated in [S1] para 10.1, banks must obtain explicit consent from customers for registering or de-registering for digital banking services, with the consent duly recorded, and must clearly indicate that SMS/email alerts will be sent to the customer's registered mobile number or email for all account operations. The passage further specifies that this information, along with terms and conditions, must be provided in clear and simple language.

As stated in [S2], the RBI's interpretation of any provision of the Directions "shall be final and binding on all concerned entities." Therefore, as a compliance officer, you can rely on the RBI's interpretation when a provision is ambiguous, as it carries binding authority within the framework of these Directions.

As stated in [S1] para 8, banks offering digital banking services must follow the "Guidelines on Outsourcing of Information Technology Services as specified in Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025 dated November 28, 2025, as amended from time to time." Additionally, [S2] para 54 specifies that any outsourced model for digital banking segments, including DBUs, must specifically comply with the relevant regulatory guidelines on outsourcing contained in the same 2025 Directions.

According to [S1] para 6.1, a commercial bank must have implemented Core Banking Solution (CBS) and enabled its public facing IT infrastructure to handle Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6) traffic to be eligible for offering view-only internet or mobile banking facilities.

According to [S1] paragraph 5, banks shall put in place comprehensive policy(ies) for all digital banking channels, keeping in account all statutory and regulatory requirements, including the management of liquidity and operational risks in the digital banking scenario.

Yes, according to [S5], the provisions of the Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions "shall be in addition to, and not in derogation of the provisions of any other laws, rules, regulations, or directions, for the time being in force." This means a commercial bank must still comply with all other applicable laws and regulations alongside these Directions.

The Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025 apply to Commercial Banks, defined as banking companies other than Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, and Local Area Banks, plus corresponding new banks and the State Bank of India, as specified under clauses (c), (da), and (nc) of Section 5 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 [S5].

The bank should consider lodging a formal complaint against the statutory auditor with the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) or Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) to examine and fix accountability [S1]. Pending disciplinary action, the complaint must be forwarded to the Reserve Bank (Department of Supervision, Central Office) and the Indian Banks' Association (IBA), after satisfying oneself of the auditor's involvement and providing an opportunity to be heard, with all procedures suitably recorded [S1]. Subsequently, the Indian Banks' Association will prepare a caution list of such auditors for circulation among lenders [S1].
As stated in [S2], the responsibility for reporting correct information and ensuring the accuracy of facts and figures rests with the reporting bank.

According to [S1], the bar on additional credit facility to the wilful defaulter or any entity with which the wilful defaulter is associated shall be effective for a period of one year after the name of the wilful defaulter has been removed from the List of Wilful Defaulters by the lenders. This one-year restriction applies specifically to the "bar on additional credit facility" as distinct from the five-year prohibition on granting credit facilities for floating new ventures mentioned elsewhere in the same paragraph.

According to paragraph 15(1) of the RBI (Commercial Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025, a borrower or guarantor classified as a wilful defaulter must be removed from the List of Wilful Defaulters after implementation of a resolution plan under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code or the RBI (Commercial Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025, specifically when the resolution results in a change in the management and control of the entity or business enterprise. [S1]

A commercial bank must put in place a transparent mechanism for the entire process of identification of wilful defaulters so that the penal provisions are applied in a fair manner and the scope for discretion is obviated. [S1]

As stated in [S1], a commercial bank must submit information on wilful defaulters to credit information companies at monthly intervals. The report, filed in Annex II, must include a list of wilful defaulters (LWD) for suit-filed accounts and a list of LWD for non-suit-filed accounts.

Before transferring a defaulted loan with outstanding of ₹30 lakh, the bank must internally conduct a comprehensive investigation from a wilful default perspective [S1]. The process need not necessarily involve a two-stage committee, but should ensure a thorough examination of wilful default aspects [S1]. If wilful default is observed, the bank must complete the classification of the borrower as a wilful defaulter as per Paragraph 5 and report it to credit information companies before the transfer [S1].

As per [S1] para 21(2), a commercial bank must forward the details of third parties involved in wilful defaults (where they played a vital role in credit sanction/disbursement and were negligent or facilitated the default) to the Indian Banks' Association (IBA) for records, regardless of the bank's membership status; IBA then prepares caution lists and circulates them to all regulated entities of the Reserve Bank, who must consider this aspect before assigning any work to such third parties. Furthermore, [S1] para 21(3) requires the bank, before reporting to IBA, to satisfy itself of the third party's involvement and provide them with an opportunity to be heard, following due process that shall be suitably recorded.

Yes. According to [S1], paragraph 10(2), "When a default happens in making payment / repayment by the principal debtor, a bank shall be able to proceed against the guarantor even without exhausting the remedies against the principal debtor."

Yes, the Reserve Bank of India can issue necessary clarifications on the application and interpretation of the Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters Directions. As provided in paragraph 24 of the Directions [S2], the RBI's interpretation of any provision shall be final and binding.

According to [S1], a commercial bank must report to credit information companies the details of guarantors who fail to honour their commitments when invoked, classifying them as large defaulters or wilful defaulters as the case may be, with details reported as per Annex I and II.

The Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025, apply to commercial banks, defined as banking companies, corresponding new banks, and State Bank of India under subsections (c), (da), and (nc) of section 5 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, while explicitly excluding Small Finance Banks, Local Area Banks, Payments Banks, and Regional Rural Banks [S1].
According to [S1], a bank shall require their internal auditors to specifically look into adherence to instructions for classifying a borrower as a wilful defaulter.

According to [S1] para 13(1), a commercial bank may remove a wilful defaulter's name from the List of Wilful Defaulters only after the borrower has fully paid the compromise amount. [S1] para 13(2) further specifies that until full payment is made, the borrower's name shall not be removed from the LWD even if the outstanding amount falls below the ₹25 lakh threshold or as notified by RBI from time to time.

As stated in [S1], "The provisions of these Directions shall be in addition to, and not in derogation of the provisions of any other laws, rules, regulations, or directions, for the time being in force." This means the Directions complement rather than override existing legal frameworks.

[S2]

As stated in [S1], a commercial bank covered under the Reserve Bank – Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (RB-IOS) shall comply with the directions provided under the said Scheme. This is the compliance obligation specified for such entities under the Credit Information Reporting framework.
The CICRA provides statutory backing for sharing of credit information by a CI with CICs, subject to conditions stipulated therein. [S1]

According to [S1], a commercial bank must undertake a half yearly review of the Data Quality Index (DQI) for all segments. This review is conducted every six months to improve the quality of data submitted to CICs.

A bank shall include in their loan policies/credit appraisal processes suitable provisions for obtaining Credit Information Reports (CIRs) from one or more Credit Information Companies (CICs) so that credit decisions are based on credit information available in the system. [S1]
According to [S1] para 4, ‘Company’ means a company defined under section 3 of the Companies Act, 1956 or corresponding section under the Companies Act, 2013.
As stated in [S1] paragraph 9, the standardised format for the commercial segment is Form 2: Uniform Credit Reporting Format (Commercial) – for commercial segment.

This means commercial banks must continue complying with all other applicable laws and RBI directions alongside these Directions.
According to [S2], the Technical Working Group must convene its meetings at least once in a calendar year.

The TWG comprises representatives from Public Sector Banks, Private Sector Banks, Foreign Banks, Primary (Urban) Cooperative Banks (UCBs), Regional Rural Banks (RRBs), All India Notified Financial Institutions (AIFIs), Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs), Housing Finance Companies (HFCs), Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs), India Banks’ Association (IBA), Micro Finance Institutions Network (MFIN), Sa-Dhan, and CICs. [S2]

According to [S1], if a term is not defined in the RBI Credit Information Reporting Directions, a commercial bank should first refer to CICRA, 2005, the Credit Information Companies Rules, 2006, and the CIC Regulations for its meaning. If the term remains undefined there, it should then be interpreted using the meanings assigned in the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, or the Companies Act, 2013.

According to [S2], the Credit Information Reporting Directions apply to Commercial Banks defined as banking companies "other than Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, and Local Area Banks," meaning these three types of banks are explicitly excluded from coverage.

As per [S1] para 34(2), a commercial bank acting as a CI must designate a dedicated nodal point/official for contact with CICs, furnish their details (email ID, telephone/mobile number) to CICs, and inform CICs of any changes within five calendar days.

Additionally, the Government of India nominee director and directors nominated under Section 19(f) of the SBI Act or Section 9(3)(c) of the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970/1980 are explicitly ineligible to serve on the Committee, per [S1] para 22(2).

According to [S1], a bank must obtain regulatory approval for Additional Roles or Responsibilities of MD&CEO/CEO in terms of Section 10B(8) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, by submitting the request through the Pravaah Portal (https://pravaah.rbi.org.in).

According to [S1], no person shall continue as the MD&CEO/CEO or WTD of a PVB beyond the age of 70 years. Furthermore, a PVB's Board may prescribe a lower retirement age as part of its internal policy.

As stated in [S1] para 11, a Public Sector Bank's Board shall institutionalise discussions between its management and the Board on the quality of internal control systems. The Board is specifically required to pay attention to creating and sustaining a culture of control. These obligations ensure ongoing oversight and improvement of the bank's internal control environment.

According to [S1] para 38(ii), the minimum aggregate working capital limit from the banking system that triggers nominee director eligibility for a unit showing signs of incipient sickness is ₹1 crore and above.

According to [S1] para 8, a PSB’s Board must fulfil four major roles: overseeing the risk profile of the PSB, monitoring the integrity of its business and control mechanisms, ensuring expert management, and maximising the interests of its stakeholders.
Yes, according to [S1] para 35, a Public Sector Bank may entrust the Chief Vigilance Officer with portfolios including Inspection and Audit, Accounts, Planning and Development, and Legal matters.

According to [S1], paragraph 70, a bank proposing to amend its Articles of Association must obtain prior regulatory approval through the Pravaah Portal (under Section 35B of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949) before circulating the draft amendments to its shareholders or convening a meeting of the shareholders in this regard.

Yes, according to [S1], the Master Direction must be read along with other relevant governing statutes. Furthermore, [S2] confirms that the Directions operate in addition to, and not in derogation of, any other laws in force, meaning commercial banks are required to interpret and apply the Directions together with other applicable statutes.

According to [S1], any action taken under the repealed directions continues to be governed by those same provisions, and the repeal does not affect any rights, obligations, liabilities, penalties, or investigations incurred thereunder. Approvals or acknowledgments granted under the repealed directions are also deemed governed by them.
According to [S2](ii), Private Sector Banks are governed by provisions specified in Chapter III of the RBI's Governance Directions for commercial banks.

Additionally, [S1] para 21(4) specifies that RMCB meetings shall be chaired by an independent director who shall not be the Chair of the Board, so the Chair can be a member but not the meeting chair.
According to [S1] para 65, a proposal for appointing a new MD&CEO must be submitted to RBI at least four months before the expiry of the term of office of the present incumbent.

A bank may determine interest rates on advances in foreign currency in accordance with a comprehensive policy on interest rates on advances that must be duly approved by the Board of Directors or any committee of the Board to which powers have been delegated [S1].

No, a commercial bank cannot apply different tenor premiums to different borrowers or loan categories for the same residual tenor. [S1] states that the tenor premium will be uniform for all types of loans for a given residual tenor. [S2] further specifies that the change in tenor premium shall be uniform for all types of loans for a given residual tenor.
Yes, according to [S1] paragraph 7, the interest-rate directions in paragraph 6 also apply to rupee advances granted against FCNR(B) deposits to a third party.

According to [S3] para 5, an "External benchmark rate" includes: (1) Reserve Bank of India policy Repo Rate; (2) Government of India Three-months and Six-months Treasury Bill yields published by Financial Benchmarks India Private Ltd (FBIL); and (3) Any other benchmark market interest rate published by FBIL.

As stated in [S1] para 38, the interest rate under an external benchmark shall be reset at least once in three months. This reset frequency applies regardless of the loan's tenor, as the external benchmark reset is governed by a fixed three-month cycle.

According to paragraph 28 of the RBI Directions, a bank's Board-approved policy on spread must include principles for determining the quantum of each component of spread, the range of spread for a given borrower/loan category, and delegation of powers for loan pricing [S1]. Furthermore, paragraph 30 specifies that the policy must adopt the broad components of business strategy and credit risk premium, arrived at considering market competition, embedded options, liquidity, credit risk rating, expected losses, and collaterals [S2].

The in-progress action of sanctioning a loan and setting its interest rate continues to be governed by the earlier repealed interest-rate directions for Commercial Banks, as [S1] states: "any action taken or purported to have been taken, or initiated under the repealed Directions, instructions, or guidelines shall continue to be governed by the provisions thereof." This savings clause ensures that the bank's initiated steps remain subject to the original directions despite their repeal.
According to [S1], the MCLR prevailing on the date of first disbursement, whether partial or full, shall be applicable till the next reset date.
As stated in [S1] para 14, a bank shall review the Base Rate at least once in a quarter. [S3] para 39 further specifies that the bank must continue to review and publish the Base Rate as hitherto.

Under [S2] paragraph 6(1), a commercial bank must maintain a comprehensive interest rate policy on advances that is duly approved by the Board of Directors or any committee to which powers have been delegated, and this policy must include the pricing of microfinance loans. This policy serves as the governing framework for determining interest rates on all advances, as further detailed in the subsequent sub-paragraphs of [S2] paragraph 6.

According to [S1] paragraph 13, a commercial bank may calculate the cost of funds using the average cost of funds, the marginal cost of funds, or any other methodology currently in vogue. The chosen method must be reasonable and transparent, consistent, and made available for supervisory review or scrutiny as and when required, and if a card rate for deposits of one or more tenors is used, those deposits must constitute the largest share of the bank's deposit base.

According to [S2], existing loans and credit limits linked to the Base Rate or BPLR "shall continue till repayment or renewal, as the case may be," and do not automatically convert to MCLR. Instead, "existing borrowers shall have the option to move to the MCLR linked loan at mutually acceptable terms," meaning they remain under the old benchmark unless the borrower opts to switch.

According to [S2] paragraph 29(1), a commercial bank may increase the credit risk premium charged to an existing borrower if there is deterioration in the customer's credit risk profile (or a change in tenor premium). The stipulation explicitly permits such an increase on account of deterioration in the credit risk profile, though it does not apply to loans under consortium or multiple banking arrangements.

According to paragraph 15, all floating rate rupee loans sanctioned and renewed on or after April 1, 2016 shall be priced with reference to the Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR), which is the internal benchmark for such purposes. [S1]

As per [S1] para 18, negative carry on mandatory CRR with nil returns on CRR balances is calculated as Required CRR × (marginal cost) / (1 - CRR), where the marginal cost of funds is determined as outlined in [S2] para 17.

No, the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025 do not override or replace other existing laws and regulations applicable to commercial banks. According to para 48 [S3], the provisions of these Directions shall be "in addition to, and not in derogation of the provisions of any other laws, rules, regulations, or directions, for the time being in force."

As stated in [S1], the Customer Acceptance Policy shall not result in denial of a financial facility to members of the general public, especially those who are financially or socially disadvantaged, including the Persons with Disabilities (PwDs). The NBFC shall not reject an application for onboarding or periodic updation of KYC without application of mind, and any rejection must be duly recorded with reasons.

Paragraph 8 of the NBFC Know Your Customer guidelines [S1] explicitly states that every NBFC which is part of a group shall implement group-wide programmes against money laundering and terror financing, including group-wide policies for sharing information and safeguards to prevent tipping-off.

As per [S1] para 41, the NBFC must carry out a periodic review of the risk categorisation of customer accounts at least once every six months. This review is required to align monitoring with risk categories and to determine the need for applying enhanced due diligence measures.

As per [S1] para 38(1), an NBFC is not required to identify and verify the beneficial owners of a legal person customer when the customer or the owner of the controlling interest is an entity listed on a stock exchange in India, an entity resident in jurisdictions notified by the Central Government and listed on stock exchanges in such jurisdictions, or a subsidiary of such listed entities.

According to [S1], the Board of Directors of the NBFC, or any committee to which the Board has delegated power, shall duly approve the KYC policy. This explicitly authorizes the Board to delegate the approval responsibility to a committee.

According to [S1], if a non-profit organisation customer is not already registered on the DARPAN Portal of NITI Aayog, the NBFC shall register the details on the DARPAN Portal. The NBFC must also maintain such registration records for a period of five years after the business relationship ends or the account is closed, whichever is later.

An NBFC must implement a policy framework that ensures compliance with the PML Act/Rules and provides a bulwark against money laundering and terrorist financing risks, while considering best international practices such as FATF standards [S2]. The NBFC must also carry out periodic Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment exercises to identify, assess, and mitigate risks for clients, products, and delivery channels [S3]. If part of a group, it must further implement group-wide anti-money laundering and terror financing programmes with policies for information sharing and confidentiality safeguards [S1].

According to [S1], the NBFC shall verify the UNSC Sanctions Lists and domestic terrorism schedules on a daily basis. [S2] further requires the NBFC to verify the UNSCR 1718 Sanctions List every day. Therefore, an NBFC must check these lists daily.

According to paragraph 34 of the NBFC KYC guidelines [S1], an NBFC must obtain certified copies of: (1) the registration certificate, (2) the partnership deed, (3) the PAN of the partnership firm, (4) documents specifying beneficial owners, managers, officers, or employees with transaction authority, (5) the names of all partners, and (6) the registered office and principal place of business address.

According to [S1], where an NBFC forms a suspicion of money laundering or terrorist financing and reasonably believes that performing the CDD process will tip off the customer, it shall not pursue the CDD process and instead file an STR with FIU-IND.

According to [S2] para 23(1), an NBFC requires an individual's Aadhaar number where they are desirous of receiving any benefit or subsidy under section 7 of the Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies Benefits and Services) Act, 2016, or where they voluntarily submit their Aadhaar number to the NBFC or a relevant entity notified under the first proviso to sub-section (1) of section 11A of the PML Act. [S1] Explanation 4 further clarifies that Aadhaar number is not mandatory for KYC purposes; it is only required in the above case, and in all other cases, customers may provide it voluntarily.

According to [S1] para 31, an NBFC shall obtain any two of the following documents or equivalent e-documents as proof of business/activity for a sole proprietary firm: (1) Registration certificate including Udyam Registration Certificate (URC) issued by the Government; (2) Certificate/licence issued by municipal authorities under the Shop and Establishment Act; (3) Sales and income tax returns; (4) CST/VAT/GST certificate; (5) Certificate/registration document issued by Sales Tax/Service Tax/Professional Tax authorities; (6) IEC issued by the office of DGFT or licence/certificate of practice issued by any professional body incorporated under a statute; (7) Complete Income Tax Return (not just the acknowledgement) in the name of the sole proprietor where the firm's income is reflected, duly authenticated/acknowledged by the Income Tax authorities; and (8) Utility bills such as electricity, water, landline telephone bills, etc.

According to [S1], an NBFC must verify the UNSCR 1718 Sanctions List every day to account for any modifications and ensure compliance with the Implementation of Security Council Resolution on Democratic People’s Republic of Korea Order, 2017, as amended from time to time by the Central Government.

Under the RBI's KYC Directions, [S1] states that the NBFC shall undertake ongoing due diligence of customers to ensure that their transactions are consistent with their knowledge about the customers, customers' business and risk profile, and the source of funds/wealth. [S5] further defines 'On-going Due Diligence' as regular monitoring of transactions in accounts for these same criteria.
Yes. [S1] paragraph 46(2) states that an NBFC has the option to hold 'pooled' accounts managed by professional intermediaries on behalf of entities like mutual funds or pension funds.

[S1] states that an NBFC applies the CDD procedure at the UCIC level, so if an existing KYC-compliant customer desires to open another account or avail of any other product or service from the same NBFC, there shall be no need for a fresh CDD exercise as far as identification of the customer is concerned.

According to [S2], an NBFC treats a loan as commercial real estate exposure if the prospects for repayment or recovery in case of default depend primarily on the cash flows generated by the asset, such as through lease/rental payments or its sale. Additionally, [S2] specifies that loans for third dwelling unit onwards to an individual are automatically classified as CRE exposure.

As per [S1] para 107(6), the maximum interval allowed between the sanction of a demand or call loan and the first mandatory performance review is six months. The passage specifies: "A cut-off date, for review of performance of the loan, not exceeding six months commencing from the date of sanction."

According to [S1] para 30(1), EMI programmes on credit cards for NBFCs are governed specifically by the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025, and such transactions are explicitly excluded from the Credit Facilities Directions, meaning they do not fall within that chapter's scope.

According to [S1], paragraph 11(1), the cooling-off period for a digital loan must not be less than one day, as determined by the NBFC in terms of their credit policy. The borrower is given an explicit option to exit the loan by paying the principal and proportionate APR without penalty during this initial period.
The maximum annual household income for a loan to qualify as a microfinance loan for an NBFC is ₹3,00,000. [S1]

Per [S3], NBFCs must make prescribed disclosures in the 'Notes to Accounts' section of their financial statements. [S1] and [S2] similarly require disclosures "in the ‘Notes to Accounts’" as specified in the RBI Directions. Thus, the 'Notes to Accounts' is the designated location for all such required disclosures.

According to [S1], an NBFC shall not avail loans by re-pledging gold or silver pledged to it by its borrowers. Therefore, an NBFC cannot obtain a loan by re-pledging gold or silver that its own borrowers have pledged to it.

No, an NBFC cannot enter into a default loss guarantee arrangement with a lender that is not acting as an LSP. According to [S1] para 19, an NBFC may enter into DLG arrangements only with an LSP / other lender engaged as an LSP. This restriction means that DLG arrangements with non-LSP lenders would not be permitted under the RBI directions.

The borrower must not be in any financial distress, and the project loan exposure must be classified as standard. [S1] states that so long as these conditions are met—referencing the RBI (Non-Banking Financial Companies–Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 for the indicative list of signs of financial difficulty—providing a commercially priced PCE to enhance a bond issue replacing the project loan would not amount to restructuring.

An NBFC classifies financed projects into three stages—Design phase, Construction phase, and Operational phase—under RBI prudential guidelines [S1]. The Design phase starts with the project's genesis and includes designing, planning, and obtaining all applicable clearances/approvals until financial closure [S1].

According to [S1] para 106, an NBFC with asset size of ₹100 crore and above must maintain a loan-to-value (LTV) ratio of 50 per cent when lending against listed shares, and any shortfall due to share price movements must be corrected within seven working days.
According to [S2] para 26(2), an NBFC that provides a default loss guarantee (DLG) must deduct the full outstanding amount of the DLG from its regulatory capital.

According to [S1] para 5, an NBFC’s credit policy must cover specified areas “to the extent such activities are undertaken by it.” This qualifier means the policy only needs to address project finance or housing finance if the NBFC actually undertakes those activities. Therefore, if an NBFC does not offer project finance or housing finance, its credit policy is not required to address those areas.

No, according to [S1] (NBFC - Credit Facilities, para 71), approvals/clearances contingent upon project milestone achievement shall not be treated as applicable mandatory pre-requisites at the time of financial closure, as they only become applicable once the specified milestones are met (e.g., consent to operate a boiler can only be applied for after the construction of a boiler).

According to [S1] para 108, an NBFC must stipulate that the builder/developer disclose the name(s) of the mortgagee entity in on-site pamphlets/brochures/display boards, append mortgage details in advertisements published in newspapers/magazines, and indicate in brochures that they will provide a No Objection Certificate/permission from the mortgagee entity for sale of flats/property if required. Furthermore, the NBFC shall ensure compliance with these stipulations and release funds only upon fulfillment of these requirements.

According to [S1], the first auction of gold or silver collateral must be conducted physically in the same district in which the lending branch is located. If the first auction fails, the NBFC may then conduct the auction in an adjoining district or online.

[S1] states that a recovery agent must carry a copy of the notice, the authorisation letter from the NBFC, and the identity card issued by the NBFC or the agency. Furthermore, if the recovery agency is changed during the process, the new agent must also carry the notice and authorisation letter along with the identity card.

Yes, according to passage [S1], Self-Regulatory Organisations may publish the range of interest rates on microfinance loans charged by their members operating in a district as part of their awareness campaigns. [S1] explicitly states: "As part of their awareness campaigns, Self-Regulatory Organisations (SROs) / other industry associations may publish the range of interest rates on microfinance loans charged by their members operating in a district."

According to [S1], an NBFC must include in the assay certificate the purity (in terms of carats), gross weight of the eligible collateral pledged, net weight of gold or silver content, deductions relating to weight of stones, lac, alloy, strings, fastenings, etc., any damage, breakage or defects noticed in the collateral, an image of the collateral, and the value of collateral calculated as per the RBI (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, at the time of sanction.

[S2] states that at the time of sanction, the NBFC must prepare a certificate or e-certificate in duplicate on its letterhead regarding the assay of the collateral, specifying the purity in carats, gross and net weight, deductions for stones/alloy/strings, any noticed damage or defects, an image of the collateral, and its calculated value. One copy of the certificate must be kept as part of the loan documents, and the other copy must be given to the borrower under their acknowledgement.

According to [S2], an NBFC must announce the auction to the public by issuing advertisements in at least two newspapers, one in the regional language and another in a national daily, as part of implementing a transparent auction procedure. This requirement ensures public notice and participation in the auction process for gold and silver collateral.

An NBFC must furnish a copy of the loan agreement along with a copy of all enclosures quoted in the loan agreement to all borrowers at the time of sanction or disbursement of the loan [S2][S3]. Furthermore, digitally signed documents such as the Key Fact Statement, summary of the loan product, sanction letter, terms and conditions, account statements, and privacy policies must be automatically sent to the borrower's registered email or SMS upon execution of the loan contract [S1].
According to [S1], an NBFC must place a report on unclaimed gold and/or silver collateral before the Customer Service Committee or the Board at half-yearly intervals for review.

An NBFC is required to release all securities held as collateral upon repayment of all dues or realization of the outstanding loan amount, subject to any legitimate right or lien, as stated in [S2] para 17. Furthermore, [S1] para 58 mandates that pledged eligible collateral must be released on the same day but within a maximum of seven working days after full repayment or settlement.
An NBFC shall store the collateral only in its branches which are manned by its employees and having safe deposit vaults fit for storing gold and silver [S1].

Loan application forms shall include necessary information affecting the borrower's interest, so that a meaningful comparison with the terms and conditions offered by another lender can be made, and an informed decision can be taken. The forms must also indicate the documents required to be submitted. [S1]

An NBFC shall display on its website the methodology adopted by it for determination of net weight of the gold and silver content of the eligible collateral and the price used to value the gold and silver content of the eligible collateral for determination of LTV ratio. [S1]

According to paragraph 12 of the Non-Banking Financial Companies - Fraud Risk Management Directions, the Applicable NBFC shall disclose the amount related to fraud reported in the company for the year in its Financial Statements – Notes to Accounts. [S1]

NBFCs in the Upper Layer and Middle Layer must develop or strengthen their Early Warning System by identifying suitable indicators and parameterising them for monitoring other financial/non-credit related transactions, as required under [S1]. They must also continuously upgrade the system to enhance its integrity and robustness, and test its effectiveness periodically, as further specified in [S1].

Yes, according to [S1], any fraud risk management actions taken under the repealed NBFC directions continue to be governed by the provisions thereof, and the repeal does not invalidate them. The passage explicitly states such actions remain valid and enforceable as if the directions had not been repealed.

[S1], paragraph 38 states that the penal measures detailed in Paragraphs 35 and 36 shall not be applicable to entities or business enterprises after implementation of the Resolution Plan under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) or the aforesaid resolution framework.

According to [S1], when an account is identified as a fraud by an Applicable NBFC, the borrowal accounts of other group companies sharing one or more promoter(s) or whole-time director(s) shall also be subjected to examination by Regulated Entities (REs) concerned from the fraud angle under these Directions.

According to [S1], an NBFC may close fraud cases using the ‘Closure Module’ only after the fraud cases pending with LEAs/Court are disposed of and the examination of staff accountability is completed. Additionally, [S2] allows closing reported fraud cases involving amounts up to ₹25 lakh, for limited statistical/reporting purposes, if staff accountability has been examined and disciplinary action taken, and either the investigation/charge-sheet has been pending for over three years from the FIR date, or the trial has not commenced/been pending for over three years from the FIR date.

[S1] para 25 states that the Applicable NBFC shall use an external audit or an internal audit as per its Board approved Policy for further investigation in such accounts where there is a suspicion or indication of wrongdoing or fraudulent activity.

According to [S1] para 54, an Applicable NBFC must complete the investigation from the fraud angle before transferring the loan account or credit facility to other lenders or Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs). The passage explicitly requires this completion prior to any transfer, and if a fraud is concluded, the NBFC must report it to RBI before selling the accounts.

[S1] paragraph 57 states that an NBFC must report instances of robbery or attempted theft to the RBI immediately, and not later than seven days from their occurrence. The report must be submitted in the prescribed ‘Return on Bank Robberies, Dacoities, Thefts and Burglaries (RBR)’ format via email to fmgconbfc@rbi.org.in.

An NBFC may withdraw an FMR or remove a perpetrator's name under exceptional circumstances, provided there is due justification and approval from an official at least in the rank of a director [S1]. Additionally, if such withdrawal or removal is necessitated by court directions, the NBFC may act immediately, after which the case must be placed before an official in the rank of WTD for information [S3].

According to [S1], paragraph 51, NBFCs are allowed to close reported fraud cases involving an amount up to ₹25 lakh for limited statistical/reporting purposes, provided the specified conditions on investigation and trial status are met.

As stated in [S1], the internal audit in an Applicable NBFC must cover controls and processes involved in the prevention, detection, classification, monitoring, reporting, closure, and withdrawal of fraud cases, as well as weaknesses in the fraud risk management framework, including delays in reporting, non-reporting, staff accountability examination, and prudential provisioning.

According to [S1], the minimum fraud amount that must be reported to law enforcement agencies is ₹1 lakh or more. [S1] explicitly states: "The Applicable NBFC is, however, advised to mandatorily report incidents of fraud involving an amount of ₹1 lakh or more to LEAs."
According to [S1], the Applicable NBFC shall frame a policy on engagement of external auditors covering aspects such as due diligence, competency and track record of the auditors, among others.

Yes, according to [S1], the Applicable NBFC may incorporate necessary terms and conditions in its agreements with third-party service providers to hold them accountable in situations where wilful negligence / malpractice by them is found to be a causative factor for fraud.

According to [S1], paragraph 34 of the NBFC Fraud Risk Management Directions states that in cases involving very senior executives of the Applicable NBFC (such as the MD & CEO / Executive Director / Executives of equivalent rank), the ACB shall initiate examination of their accountability and place it before the Board. Such executives shall not participate in the meeting of the Board / ACB / SCBMF in which their accountability is to be considered. However, if the Applicable NBFC is in the public sector, such cases shall also be referred to the Advisory Board for Banking and Financial Frauds (ABBFF).
